content: The Orange County Health Department operates as a division of the Florida Department of Health, tasked with safeguarding the health and safety of both residents and visitors in Orange County, Florida. The county has a daytime population of approximately 1.5 million people and attracts an estimated 51 million visitors annually, largely due to major attractions such as Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando, and SeaWorld. The county seat is Orlando, Florida. The Orange County Health Department oversees a jurisdiction with a population larger than that of eight U.S. states and the District of Columbia. Its responsibilities encompass a wide range of public health services, including epidemiology, investigation of foodborne, zoonotic, and waterborne diseases, emergency preparedness, bioterrorism response, communicable disease control, health promotion and education, school health programs, women’s health services, public health dentistry, oral health, the WIC (Women, Infants, and Children) nutrition program, vaccine-preventable disease management, efforts to eliminate health disparities, issuance of vital records, and environmental health protection. In 2006, the department established the first hospital-based vital records office in the United States at Winter Park Memorial Hospital. The department has contributed to public health research and education through publications, including investigations of foodborne, waterborne, zoonotic, and other infectious diseases in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). Additionally, it has developed storyboards with graphics in toolkits, published by the Public Health Foundation in Washington, D.C., to demonstrate how quality improvement initiatives have enhanced public health outcomes for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and HIV. The WIC and nutrition program staff collaborated with the Department of Health to publish a children’s book titled The Whole Grain Choo-Choo Train, which educates young children about healthy eating habits and nutrition. In 2007, the deaths of three children in or near Orange County due to primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a rare and fatal infection, prompted a public health investigation in collaboration with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). PAM is caused by the amoeba Naegleria fowleri, which enters the brain through the nasal passages, typically resulting in death. This waterborne infection is associated with swimming or water sports in freshwater bodies or inadequately chlorinated swimming pools. The incidence of Naegleria fowleri infections may increase with global climate change, as the organism thrives in warm water. Over the past 45 years, Orange County has reported 12 cases of PAM, out of 25 cases recorded in the state of Florida. Globally, approximately 200 cases of PAM had been documented as of 1990, with occurrences reported even in colder climates such as the United Kingdom and Belgium. In 2007, additional cases were reported in Texas and Arizona. The Orange County Health Department, in collaboration with the Florida Department of Health and the CDC, has also investigated other waterborne diseases, including giardiasis, cyclosporiasis, and cryptosporidiosis. Notably, techniques for identifying cyclosporiasis were first developed in Central Florida. Public health officials strongly recommend that swimmers and water sports participants wear nose plugs when engaging in freshwater activities, particularly when ambient temperatures exceed 80 degrees Fahrenheit, to reduce the risk of infection.
